doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

chapter: Marriage and freelancing in New York
title: Reputation, jingles and cheap apartments in New York
summary: Reputation from Sauter-Finegan, other bands, jingle work with Norman Leyden, and apartment rents.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So now you’re a free lance musician—
In Syracuse. Eventually you made the move to New York City — I’m talking okay, so I’m talking what, 40— I’m sorry, 60—
‘67 I moved to Potsdam to teach.
Okay. But I want to talk about New York City a little more if you don’t mind.
Sure. I love New York City. My favorite restaurants.
As a free lance musician, what’s the best way for you to — I’m talking in general — get your reputation out there?

I was lucky I had a reputation before I got to New York. I had a reputation from the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra from the ‘50s. I was in New York in ‘48 but that was sporadically. I didn’t settle in New York until ‘53, and that was with the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra. And my name had gotten around from playing with that band, although I had played with other bands, well I played with Ray McKinley’s band after that. I played with Tito Puente, Tito Rodriguez, Sonny Dunham, a bunch of bands. Some — I only remember one, the Sauter-Finegan Orchestra.
Was the recording scene pretty healthy in the ‘50s once you got out and started to get into studio work?

It was pretty steady at that particular time, but I had gotten to know some other people, Norm and Jimmy Leyden, and then I was doing a lot of jingles, which is not the greatest musically, but monetarily it sustained me. When I got married I made sixty dollars a week doing two television shows with Norman Leyden. Thirty a week for each television show. But that was a lifesaver. Norm and Jimmy kept me going there for many years.
Well you told me earlier that your first apartment in New York cost—

My second apartment cost seventy dollars a month. And my third apartment cost eighty- five dollars a month. When I left New York it was two hundred and eighty-five dollars a month, but I don’t complain one bit.
